decks.name: AI Engineering Hub — Roadmap Q&A (math, LLMs, RAG, agents, MCP, fine-tuning)

cards.front: What is AI engineering, and how is it different from classical ML engineering?
cards.back: Building applications on top of pre-trained foundation models (prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, eval, serving) instead of training models from scratch on your own data.

cards.front: What is a vector?
cards.back: An ordered list of numbers; in ML it represents a data point or an embedding in n-dimensional space.

cards.front: What is a dot product and why does it matter in ML?
cards.back: Sum of element-wise products of two vectors; it measures alignment and is the core of similarity search and attention scores.

cards.front: What is cosine similarity?
cards.back: Dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths; measures the angle between them, ignoring magnitude. Used to compare embeddings.

cards.front: What is a matrix multiplication doing in a neural network?
cards.back: Applying a linear transformation: every layer multiplies its input vector by a weight matrix, then adds a bias.

cards.front: What is a gradient?
cards.back: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter; it points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.

cards.front: What is gradient descent?
cards.back: Repeatedly nudging parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient to reduce the loss.

cards.front: What is a learning rate?
cards.back: The step size multiplied against the gradient on every update; too high diverges, too low crawls.

cards.front: What is backpropagation?
cards.back: The chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss backward to every weight, to compute all gradients in one pass.

cards.front: What is a loss function?
cards.back: A number measuring how wrong the model's output is; training minimizes it. Cross-entropy is the standard loss for language models.

cards.front: What is probability versus likelihood?
cards.back: Probability: how likely an outcome is given fixed parameters. Likelihood: how plausible parameters are given observed data.

cards.front: What is a softmax?
cards.back: Turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1 by exponentiating and normalizing.

cards.front: What is the normal (Gaussian) distribution and why is it everywhere?
cards.back: A bell curve defined by mean and variance; sums of many small random effects tend toward it (central limit theorem).

cards.front: What is overfitting?
cards.back: The model memorizes the training set and performs worse on new data; fix with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.

cards.front: What is a train/validation/test split?
cards.back: Train on one slice, tune hyperparameters on validation, report final numbers once on the untouched test slice.

cards.front: What is a neural network?
cards.back: Stacked layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent to approximate a function.

cards.front: What is an activation function and name three?
cards.back: A nonlinearity applied after each linear layer so the network can model curves; ReLU, GELU, sigmoid.

cards.front: What is a token?
cards.back: The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word piece, character chunk, or symbol produced by a tokenizer (roughly 4 characters of English).

cards.front: What is a tokenizer such as BPE?
cards.back: Byte Pair Encoding merges the most frequent byte pairs into a vocabulary of sub-word tokens so any text can be encoded.

cards.front: What is an embedding?
cards.back: A learned dense vector representing a token, sentence, or document so that similar meanings sit close together.

cards.front: What does an LLM actually predict?
cards.back: A probability distribution over the next token given all previous tokens; text is generated one token at a time.

cards.front: What is a transformer?
cards.back: The neural architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked blocks of self-attention plus feed-forward layers, trained to predict the next token.

cards.front: What is self-attention?
cards.back: Each token builds a query, key, and value; it scores its query against every other token's key and takes a weighted sum of their values to pull in context.

cards.front: What are Q, K, and V in attention?
cards.back: Query (what I am looking for), Key (what I contain), Value (what I pass along). Attention weight = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)).

cards.front: What is multi-head attention?
cards.back: Running several attention heads in parallel so each can learn a different kind of relationship, then concatenating the results.

cards.front: What is a positional encoding?
cards.back: Extra signal added to token embeddings so the transformer knows word order, since attention itself is order-blind. RoPE is the modern version.

cards.front: What is a context window?
cards.back: The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once; everything outside it is invisible to the model.

cards.front: What is a KV cache?
cards.back: Storing each token's key and value during generation so earlier tokens are not recomputed; it is why long outputs cost memory.

cards.front: What is temperature in sampling?
cards.back: A divisor on the logits before softmax; low values make output deterministic, high values make it more random.

cards.front: What is top-p (nucleus) sampling?
cards.back: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the long tail.

cards.front: What is pretraining?
cards.back: Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of raw internet text; it gives the model its knowledge and language ability.

cards.front: What is supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
cards.back: Further training on curated prompt/response pairs so the model follows instructions in a chat format.

cards.front: What is RLHF?
cards.back: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a reward model trained on human preferences steers the policy toward helpful, safe answers.

cards.front: What is DPO?
cards.back: Direct Preference Optimization: trains on preferred vs rejected answer pairs directly, without a separate reward model.

cards.front: What is GRPO?
cards.back: Group Relative Policy Optimization: samples a group of answers per prompt and rewards those above the group average; used to train reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1.

cards.front: What is a reasoning model?
cards.back: A model trained to emit a long chain of thought before the final answer, trading inference tokens for accuracy on hard problems.

cards.front: What is LoRA?
cards.back: Low-Rank Adaptation: freezes the base weights and trains small rank-r matrices added to them, cutting fine-tuning memory by 10x or more.

cards.front: What is QLoRA?
cards.back: LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model so fine-tuning fits on a single consumer GPU.

cards.front: What is quantization?
cards.back: Storing weights in fewer bits (8, 4) to shrink memory and speed up inference at a small accuracy cost; GGUF is the common local format.

cards.front: What is Unsloth?
cards.back: A library that makes LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning of open models roughly 2x faster and lighter; the hub uses it to fine-tune DeepSeek and Qwen.

cards.front: What is Ollama?
cards.back: A local runtime that downloads and serves open models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek) behind a simple HTTP API on your own machine.

cards.front: What is knowledge distillation?
cards.back: Training a small student model to imitate a large teacher model's outputs so it keeps most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.

cards.front: What is RAG?
cards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents at query time and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data instead of memory.

cards.front: What are the stages of a RAG pipeline?
cards.back: Load documents, chunk them, embed each chunk, store in a vector DB, embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks, feed them plus the question to the LLM.

cards.front: What is chunking and why does chunk size matter?
cards.back: Splitting documents into pieces before embedding; too big dilutes the embedding, too small loses context. Overlap keeps sentences intact.

cards.front: What is a vector database and name three?
cards.back: A store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over embeddings; Qdrant, Milvus, Chroma (also pgvector in Postgres).

cards.front: What is hybrid search?
cards.back: Combining dense vector similarity with keyword (BM25) search so exact terms and semantic matches both score.

cards.front: What is a reranker?
cards.back: A cross-encoder that re-scores the retrieved chunks against the query to put the best ones first before they reach the LLM.

cards.front: What is ColBERT (late interaction)?
cards.back: Embeds every token instead of the whole passage and scores by per-token max similarity; more precise retrieval than single-vector embeddings.

cards.front: What is agentic RAG?
cards.back: The model decides when and what to retrieve, can retry with a rewritten query, and can fall back to web search instead of a single fixed retrieve step.

cards.front: What is corrective RAG (CRAG)?
cards.back: Grading retrieved documents for relevance and falling back to web search or query rewriting when they are weak.

cards.front: What is a hallucination?
cards.back: A fluent but false output; mitigated with grounding (RAG), citations, lower temperature, and evaluation.

cards.front: What is an AI agent?
cards.back: An LLM running in a loop that chooses tools, observes results, and keeps going until a goal is met.

cards.front: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent (Anthropic's definition)?
cards.back: Workflow: LLM calls orchestrated by predefined code paths. Agent: the LLM itself directs its own steps and tool use dynamically.

cards.front: What is the ReAct pattern?
cards.back: Reason + Act: the model alternates between a thought, a tool call, and reading the observation until it can answer.

cards.front: What is tool calling (function calling)?
cards.back: The model emits a structured JSON call matching a declared schema; your code runs it and returns the result as the next message.

cards.front: Name five agent workflow patterns from Anthropic's Building Effective Agents.
cards.back: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.

cards.front: What is a multi-agent system?
cards.back: Several specialized agents (researcher, writer, reviewer) coordinated by an orchestrator or handoffs; CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph are frameworks for it.

cards.front: What is CrewAI?
cards.back: A Python framework where agents have a role, goal, and backstory, work on tasks, and run as a Crew (autonomous) or a Flow (event-driven, deterministic).

cards.front: What is agent memory and what are its types?
cards.back: State an agent keeps across turns or sessions: short-term (conversation), long-term (vector or graph store), episodic (past runs). Zep and Graphiti build temporal knowledge graphs for it.

cards.front: What is MCP?
cards.back: Model Context Protocol: an open standard where a client (Claude, Cursor) connects to servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts over JSON-RPC via stdio or HTTP.

cards.front: What are the three primitives an MCP server can expose?
cards.back: Tools (functions the model can call), resources (data it can read), prompts (reusable templates).

cards.front: What is A2A (agent-to-agent protocol)?
cards.back: Google's protocol for agents to discover each other through an agent card and exchange tasks, complementary to MCP's tool connections.

cards.front: What is context engineering?
cards.back: Deliberately deciding what goes into the context window each step: instructions, retrieved facts, memory, tool results, and compaction of history.

cards.front: What is prompt caching?
cards.back: Reusing the processed prefix of a prompt (system prompt, documents) across calls so you pay a fraction of the input cost and get faster responses.

cards.front: What is structured output?
cards.back: Forcing the model to return JSON matching a schema (Pydantic model) so downstream code can parse it reliably.

cards.front: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
cards.back: Using a strong model with a rubric to score another model's outputs at scale when human grading is too slow.

cards.front: What are the main RAG evaluation metrics?
cards.back: Faithfulness (answer grounded in context), answer relevance, context precision, context recall (RAGAS metrics).

cards.front: What is observability for LLM apps?
cards.back: Tracing every call with prompts, tool calls, latency, tokens, and cost (Opik, LangSmith, Langfuse) so failures can be replayed and measured.

cards.front: What is a guardrail?
cards.back: A check before or after the model (input filter, output validator, policy rule) that blocks unsafe or off-policy behavior.

cards.front: What is latency vs throughput in LLM serving?
cards.back: Latency: time to first token and per-token speed for one request. Throughput: tokens served per second across all requests. Batching trades one for the other.

cards.front: What is time to first token (TTFT)?
cards.back: Delay before the first output token appears; dominated by prompt processing (prefill) and the main driver of perceived speed.

cards.front: What is LitServe?
cards.back: A FastAPI-based serving framework from Lightning AI for deploying model and RAG endpoints with batching and autoscaling.

cards.front: What is a multimodal model?
cards.back: A model that accepts more than text (images, audio, video) in its input; Llama 3.2 Vision, Gemma 3, and Qwen 2.5 VL are open examples.

cards.front: What is OCR with a vision LLM?
cards.back: Sending an image to a multimodal model and asking for the text (or structured fields) instead of using a classical OCR engine.

cards.front: What is a knowledge graph in AI apps?
cards.back: Entities and relationships stored as a graph; GraphRAG and Graphiti use it to answer multi-hop questions that vector search misses.

cards.front: What is fine-tuning versus RAG, and when do you pick each?
cards.back: Fine-tune to change style, format, or skill; RAG to inject fresh or private facts. Start with prompting, then RAG, fine-tune last.

cards.front: What is the Zero to Hero series by Karpathy and why do it?
cards.back: Ten videos building micrograd, makemore, and GPT from scratch in Python; it is the fastest way to understand what a transformer really computes.

cards.front: What are the four 3Blue1Brown topics on LLMs?
cards.back: How neural networks learn, how transformers work, attention explained visually, how LLMs store facts in MLP layers.

cards.front: What single book does the hub recommend for AI engineering?

decks.name: AI Engineering — Answer First (name the term)

cards.front: Building applications on top of pre-trained foundation models (prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, eval, serving) instead of training models from scratch on your own data.
cards.back: What is AI engineering, and how is it different from classical ML engineering?

cards.front: An ordered list of numbers; in ML it represents a data point or an embedding in n-dimensional space.
Sum of element-wise products of two vectors; it measures alignment and is the core of similarity search and attention scores.
cards.back: What is a dot product and why does it matter in ML?

cards.front: Dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths; measures the angle between them, ignoring magnitude. Used to compare embeddings.
Applying a linear transformation: every layer multiplies its input vector by a weight matrix, then adds a bias.
cards.back: What is a matrix multiplication doing in a neural network?

cards.front: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter; it points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.
Repeatedly nudging parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient to reduce the loss.
The step size multiplied against the gradient on every update; too high diverges, too low crawls.
The chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss backward to every weight, to compute all gradients in one pass.
A number measuring how wrong the model's output is; training minimizes it. Cross-entropy is the standard loss for language models.
Probability: how likely an outcome is given fixed parameters. Likelihood: how plausible parameters are given observed data.
Turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1 by exponentiating and normalizing.
A bell curve defined by mean and variance; sums of many small random effects tend toward it (central limit theorem).
cards.back: What is the normal (Gaussian) distribution and why is it everywhere?

cards.front: The model memorizes the training set and performs worse on new data; fix with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.
Train on one slice, tune hyperparameters on validation, report final numbers once on the untouched test slice.
Stacked layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent to approximate a function.
A nonlinearity applied after each linear layer so the network can model curves; ReLU, GELU, sigmoid.
cards.back: What is an activation function and name three?

cards.front: The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word piece, character chunk, or symbol produced by a tokenizer (roughly 4 characters of English).
Byte Pair Encoding merges the most frequent byte pairs into a vocabulary of sub-word tokens so any text can be encoded.
cards.back: What is a tokenizer such as BPE?

cards.front: A learned dense vector representing a token, sentence, or document so that similar meanings sit close together.
A probability distribution over the next token given all previous tokens; text is generated one token at a time.
cards.back: What does an LLM actually predict?

cards.front: The neural architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked blocks of self-attention plus feed-forward layers, trained to predict the next token.
Each token builds a query, key, and value; it scores its query against every other token's key and takes a weighted sum of their values to pull in context.
Query (what I am looking for), Key (what I contain), Value (what I pass along). Attention weight = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)).
cards.back: What are Q, K, and V in attention?

cards.front: Running several attention heads in parallel so each can learn a different kind of relationship, then concatenating the results.
Extra signal added to token embeddings so the transformer knows word order, since attention itself is order-blind. RoPE is the modern version.
The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once; everything outside it is invisible to the model.
Storing each token's key and value during generation so earlier tokens are not recomputed; it is why long outputs cost memory.
A divisor on the logits before softmax; low values make output deterministic, high values make it more random.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the long tail.
Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of raw internet text; it gives the model its knowledge and language ability.
Further training on curated prompt/response pairs so the model follows instructions in a chat format.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a reward model trained on human preferences steers the policy toward helpful, safe answers.
Direct Preference Optimization: trains on preferred vs rejected answer pairs directly, without a separate reward model.
Group Relative Policy Optimization: samples a group of answers per prompt and rewards those above the group average; used to train reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1.
A model trained to emit a long chain of thought before the final answer, trading inference tokens for accuracy on hard problems.
Low-Rank Adaptation: freezes the base weights and trains small rank-r matrices added to them, cutting fine-tuning memory by 10x or more.
LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model so fine-tuning fits on a single consumer GPU.
Storing weights in fewer bits (8, 4) to shrink memory and speed up inference at a small accuracy cost; GGUF is the common local format.
A library that makes LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning of open models roughly 2x faster and lighter; the hub uses it to fine-tune DeepSeek and Qwen.
A local runtime that downloads and serves open models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek) behind a simple HTTP API on your own machine.
Training a small student model to imitate a large teacher model's outputs so it keeps most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents at query time and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data instead of memory.
Load documents, chunk them, embed each chunk, store in a vector DB, embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks, feed them plus the question to the LLM.
cards.back: What are the stages of a RAG pipeline?

cards.front: Splitting documents into pieces before embedding; too big dilutes the embedding, too small loses context. Overlap keeps sentences intact.
cards.back: What is chunking and why does chunk size matter?

cards.front: A store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over embeddings; Qdrant, Milvus, Chroma (also pgvector in Postgres).
cards.back: What is a vector database and name three?

cards.front: Combining dense vector similarity with keyword (BM25) search so exact terms and semantic matches both score.
A cross-encoder that re-scores the retrieved chunks against the query to put the best ones first before they reach the LLM.
Embeds every token instead of the whole passage and scores by per-token max similarity; more precise retrieval than single-vector embeddings.
The model decides when and what to retrieve, can retry with a rewritten query, and can fall back to web search instead of a single fixed retrieve step.
Grading retrieved documents for relevance and falling back to web search or query rewriting when they are weak.
A fluent but false output; mitigated with grounding (RAG), citations, lower temperature, and evaluation.
An LLM running in a loop that chooses tools, observes results, and keeps going until a goal is met.
Workflow: LLM calls orchestrated by predefined code paths. Agent: the LLM itself directs its own steps and tool use dynamically.
cards.back: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent (Anthropic's definition)?

cards.front: Reason + Act: the model alternates between a thought, a tool call, and reading the observation until it can answer.
The model emits a structured JSON call matching a declared schema; your code runs it and returns the result as the next message.
Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.
cards.back: Name five agent workflow patterns from Anthropic's Building Effective Agents.

cards.front: Several specialized agents (researcher, writer, reviewer) coordinated by an orchestrator or handoffs; CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph are frameworks for it.
A Python framework where agents have a role, goal, and backstory, work on tasks, and run as a Crew (autonomous) or a Flow (event-driven, deterministic).

cards.front:
Denise has just earned her NASM Certified Personal Trainer credential and has been hired at a health club. She hopes to attract and retain clientele to grow her business. What qualities would most help Denise be successful in her new career? Select one:
A. Creating a social media page to post client results and a hashtag that her clients can use to help grow her following
B. Providing accountability, support, feedback and guidance, and results
C. Providing a custom exercise prescription with an added meal plan for each client
D. Offering her services as an in-home trainer to people in her immediate area
cards.back: B. Providing accountability, support, feedback and guidance, and results

cards.front:
How are open-ended questions best used during the sales process?
A. The questions help a personal trainer learn about a customer's family medical history.
B. The questions are easy for the customer to answer, as they can be answered with a simple yes or no.
C. The questions identify the customer's wants, needs, fears, and desires.
D. The questions help a personal trainer learn if the customer's workout schedule fits within the personal trainer's availability.
cards.back: C. The questions identify the customer's wants, needs, fears, and desires.

cards.front:
Which component of evidence-based practice refers to a fitness professional's accumulated education, experience, and practical skills?
A. Client values and expectations
B. Individual professional expertise
C. Best external evidence
D. Number of continuing education units earned

In a SWOT analysis, which of the following would be an example of a strength?
A. Taking a workshop to learn more about sales and marketing for fitness professionals
B. Needing to learn more about marketing and sales
C. Competition from the other health clubs and training studios in the immediate area
D. Having the NASM-CPT credential

According to the NASM Code of Professional Conduct, for how long must a fitness professional maintain accurate financial, contract, appointment, and tax records? Select one:
A. 1 year
B. 6 months
C. 4 years
D. Indefinitely

Robert is a recently retired military veteran. He has earned his NASM-CPT credential because he wants to help young people prepare for the physical demands of serving in the military. Which employment options provide him with the greatest access to potential clients in all geographic locations? Select one:
A. Hosting boot camps in a local park
B. Conducting online coaching and personal training
C. Working as an in-home independent personal trainer
D. Working in a nonprofit facility
cards.back: B. Conducting online coaching and personal training

cards.front:

B. Underweight
C. Overweight

A. Unique selling proposition (USP)
B. PERT estimate
C. SWOT analysis

A. Creating handouts for clients that cover topics about fitness and wellness
B. Making time to talk to clients about how their exercise program is going
C. Taking someone shopping to purchase attire for exercise
D. Coordinating group events that are centered around physical activities
cards.back: D. Coordinating group events that are centered around physical activities

cards.front:
A Certified Personal Trainer wants to improve a client's outcome expectations for resistance training. What behavior change technique might they use? Select one:
A. Providing information on the health benefits
B. Helping them make a plan
C. Improving their confidence for their technique
D. Helping make the exercises fun
cards.back: A. Providing information on the health benefits

cards.front:

B. Follower's qualities
C. Situational factors
D. Leader's qualities

A. Coping planning
B. Action planning
C. Enlisting social support
D. Self-monitoring

Social physique anxiety is more prevalent in which population? Select one:
A. Females
B. People with a low body fat percentage
C. People with a low body mass index
D. Males

Which term best describes when someone has mixed feelings about exercise and can see both the pros and cons of participating? Select one:
A. Ambivalence
B. Unequivocal
C. Ambiguity
D. Confusion

When family members are not supportive of exercise-related behaviors, it can be viewed as which of the following? Select one:
A. Ambivalence toward exercise
B. Amotivation to exercise

D. A barrier to exercise

A. Informational support

B. As water

Which of the following nutrition topics are within the scope of practice for a Certified Personal Trainer? Select one:
A. Medical nutrition therapy as related to an individual's medical diagnoses
B. Specific nutrition recommendations for an individual's caloric, macronutrient, or micronutrient intake
C. General guidance on the importance of nutrition for health and performance
D. Meal planning with caloric or nutrient-specific guidelines for weight loss/gain or sports performance
cards.back: C. General guidance on the importance of nutrition for health and performance

cards.front:
What advice would enable a client to breathe properly? Select one:
A. Sit with an increased kyphosis and slowly breathe in through your nose while allowing your stomach to expand.
B. Sit with an increased kyphosis and slowly breathe in through your nose while minimizing abdominal movement.
C. Sit upright and slowly breathe in through your mouth while allowing your chest to expand.
D. Sit upright and slowly breathe in through your nose while allowing your stomach to expand.
cards.back: D. Sit upright and slowly breathe in through your nose while allowing your stomach to expand.

cards.front:

A. Isometric
B. Concentric
C. Eccentric
D. Isokinetic

The pathway for hormones secreted by the endocrine system may be described by which of the following? Select one:
A. The target cell releases the hormone, which travels through the bloodstream to the gland to exert a particular action.
B. The gland secretes the hormone, which travels through the bloodstream to reach a target cell, where it binds to a receptor and influences a particular action.
C. The hormone is secreted by the bloodstream and travels to the gland to exert a particular effect.
D. The gland secretes the hormone, which bypasses the bloodstream and binds to a receptor on the target cell to exert a particular action.
cards.back: B. The gland secretes the hormone, which travels through the bloodstream to reach a target cell, where it binds to a receptor and influences a particular action.

B. A substrate for anaerobic exercise

cards.back:

What does the electron transport chain (ETC) do? Select one:
A. The ETC uses an oxygen gradient to create ATP.
B. The ETC uses proteins to create hydrogen ions.
C. The ETC uses a hydrogen gradient to create ATP.
D. The ETC uses proteins to create ADP.
cards.back: C. The ETC uses a hydrogen gradient to create ATP.

B. Amino acids that must be consumed in dietary protein and cannot be created by the body

D. Amino acids that can be synthesized by the body if overall nutrition intake is adequate
cards.back: D. Amino acids that can be synthesized by the body if overall nutrition intake is adequate

B. Myosin
C. Troponin

B. Sugars that have been added to packaged foods

cards.back: C. Must be obtained in the diet, as the body is incapable of producing the nutrient on its own

cards.front:
What is the best type of plyometric exercise for a beginner client? Select one:
A. Dynamic motion
B. Small jumps
C. Fast, powerful movements
D. Explosive jumps

Your client Ethan presents with an overactive/shortened quadriceps group, which is causing the hamstrings to be underactive/lengthened. What is this phenomenon called? Select one:
A. Overtraining syndrome
B. Altered reciprocal inhibition
C. Eccentric overload
D. Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)

What are the two primary actions of the Golgi tendon organ? Select one:
A. Sense change in muscle-tendon tension and speed of tension change
B. Sense the change in muscle contraction and the speed of the nerve impulse
C. Sense the amount of eccentric tendon force and joint range of motion
D. Sense the amount of isometric tendon force and speed of shortening
cards.back: A. Sense change in muscle-tendon tension and speed of tension change

cards.front:
What is critical for personal trainers to ensure before working with a recently injured athlete? Select one:
A. A parent says training is okay.
B. The athlete can perform complex stage 3 balance exercises first.
C. The athlete has been cleared by a medical professional.
D. No balance training should be conducted following an injury.
cards.back: C. The athlete has been cleared by a medical professional.

cards.front:
What is the most important reason that a Certified Personal Trainer should make sure an older adult has been cleared by the medical provider to take part in a balance training program? Select one:
A. To make sure the program is difficult enough
B. To make sure the client isn't doing too much exercise
C. To enhance enjoyment of exercise
D. To ensure safety

You have a client seeking weight loss. What number of repetitions is most appropriate for SAQ drills? Select one:
A. 1 or 2 reps
B. 3 to 5 reps
C. 6 to 8 reps
D. 8 to 10 reps
cards.back:
B. 3 to 5 reps
C. 6 to 8 reps

cards.front:
During balance training, gluteal muscles should remain in which state to hold the body stable? Select one:
A. Concentrically contracted
B. Relaxed
C. Isometrically contracted
D. Eccentrically contracted

What is defined as the force imparted by the ground on the body when a body segment makes contact with it? Select one:
A. Ground reaction force
B. Stabilization force
C. Deceleration force
D. Acceleration force

Which of the following would not be an example of core musculature to stabilize the trunk and pelvis? Select one:
A. Pectoral group
B. Gluteal complex
C. Obliques
D. Quadratus lumborum

Training the eccentric phase of plyometric movements with a new client will help them improve which of the following? Select one:
A. Power development
B. Force production
C. Core stability
D. Landing mechanics

Which exercise is a total-body power-focused movement? Select one:
A. Two-arm push press
B. Soccer throw
C. Medicine ball chest pass
D. Front medicine ball oblique throw

What term would be used to describe the starting point of an individual's fitness level directly after an assessment has been conducted? Select one:
A. Set point
B. Action phase

What term best describes the amount of mineral content, such as calcium and phosphorous, in a segment of bone? Select one:
A. Osteopenia
B. Osteoporosis
C. Bone density
D. Sarcopenia

Which of the following options is not a benefit to all people who use balance training in their programming? Select one:
A. Improved proprioception or body awareness
B. Decreased agility-based outcomes in athletes
C. Reduced risk of ankle sprains
D. Reduced risk of falls
cards.back: B. Decreased agility-based outcomes in athletes

cards.front:
Reactive training is another common name for which type of exercise? Select one:
A. Stabilization training
B. Power training

B. All-or-nothing principle
C. Eccentric control
D. Neuromuscular efficiency

What is the Valsalva maneuver? Select one:
A. The process by which the human body strives to maintain a relatively stable equilibrium
B. The process of increasing the intensity or volume of exercise programs using a systematic and gradual approach
C. A process that involves expiring against a closed windpipe, creating additional intra-abdominal pressure and spinal stability
D. The body's ability to naturally sense its general orientation and relative position of its parts
cards.back: C. A process that involves expiring against a closed windpipe, creating additional intra-abdominal pressure and spinal stability

cards.front:
What is the primary action of the multifidus? Select one:
A. Regulate inspiration
B. Stabilize and extend the spine
C. Increase intra-abdominal pressure
D. Support the contents of the pelvis
cards.back: B. Stabilize and extend the spine

cards.front:
What does the acronym FITTE-VP, used to design aerobic (cardio) programs, represent? Select one:

B. Flexibility, intensity, training, threshold, engagement, velocity, progression
C. Flexibility, intervals, threshold, time, engagement, volume, pattern
D. Frequency, intensity, type, time, enjoyment, volume, progression
cards.back: D. Frequency, intensity, type, time, enjoyment, volume, progression

cards.front:
What are the recommended training variables for self-myofascial rolling? Select one:
A. 1 to 3 sets, hold each tender area for 2 minutes
B. 1 to 3 sets, hold each tender area for 30 seconds
C. 2 to 5 sets, hold each tender area for 5 minutes
D. 5 to 10 sets, hold each tender area for 5 seconds
cards.back:
A. 1 to 3 sets, hold each tender area for 2 minutes
B. 1 to 3 sets, hold each tender area for 30 seconds

cards.front:
What is it called when an individual performs the same task repeatedly over time, which can lead to movement dysfunction? Select one:
A. Autogenic inhibition
B. Pattern overload

A. Standing on two limbs with eyes open

C. Standing on two limbs catching a ball
D. Squatting on one limb with eyes closed
cards.back: D. Squatting on one limb with eyes closed

cards.front:

D. Strength

Of the following individuals, who would be the most suitable for being programmed SAQ (speed, agility, and quickness) exercises/movements? Select one:

B. An overweight client with adequate strength

D. A client who has been training for 1 month with adequate strength
cards.back: D. A client who has been training for 1 month with adequate strength

B. Ability to maintain zone 1 intensity for at least 45 minutes, 4 times per week
C. Ability to maintain zone 1 intensity for at least 30 minutes, 5 times per week
D. Ability to maintain zone 1 intensity for at least 30 minutes, 3 times per week
cards.back: D. Ability to maintain zone 1 intensity for at least 30 minutes, 3 times per week

D. Speed

What are the recommended training variables for dynamic stretching? Select one:

B. 1 set, 10 to 15 repetitions, 3 to 10 exercises
C. 3 to 9 sets, hold each stretch for 4 to 15 seconds, repeat for 5 to 20 repetitions

B. 1 set, 10 to 15 repetitions, 3 to 10 exercises

Most exercises and motions of the body regularly occur in which plane of motion? Select one:

Proper abdominal crunches on a stability ball allows for: Select one:

cards.front:
What blood pressure is reflective of a hypertensive crisis? Select one:
A. A systolic reading greater than 180 mm Hg and/or a diastolic reading greater than 120 mm Hg
B. A reading of 120 to 129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
C. A systolic reading of 140 mm Hg or higher or a diastolic of 90 mm Hg or higher
D. A reading of 130 to 139 mm Hg systolic or 80 to 89 mm Hg diastolic
cards.back: A. A systolic reading greater than 180 mm Hg and/or a diastolic reading greater than 120 mm Hg

cards.front:
Which of the following would be an appropriate Phase 2 superset? Select one:
A. Single-leg hops and ball push-ups
B. Power step-ups and ice skaters
C. Bench press and stability ball push-ups
D. Deadlifts and squats
cards.back: C. Bench press and stability ball push-ups

C. Pushing test
D. Shark skill test

A. Height and age

Roderick, an NASM-CPT, has submitted his application to be a personal trainer through the website of a large health club company. What will provide the best opportunity to get noticed by the hiring manager? Select one:

B. Wearing a suit and tie to the health club to drop off a resume with the hiring manager and complete an application in person
C. Posting workout videos to a social media account and tagging the health club and hiring managers

cards.front:
At her annual physical, Claire found out her blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg. According to this information, which statement is true? Select one:

B. She needs to modify her diet to bring down her blood pressure.

Which of the following best defines cholesterol? Select one:
A. A waxy, fatlike substance found in bodily cells
B. A substance that attaches itself to muscles and tendons
C. A raising of blood pressure
D. A narrowing of arteries to the heart
cards.back: A. A waxy, fatlike substance found in bodily cells

cards.front:
How can health best be defined? Select one:
A. A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
B. A combination of education, income, and occupation
C. Genetics, access to healthcare, access to preventive medicine, socioeconomic status, natural disasters, and the built environment
D. A process by which the human body continually strives to maintain a relatively stable equilibrium in relation to the surrounding environment and the regular tasks it is required to perform
cards.back: A. A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity

A new client is having trouble managing her busy schedule and has cancelled her last 3 personal training sessions. What is the best option for the fitness professional? Select one:
A. Refund the remaining sessions and actively search for a new client.
B. Help the client determine her barriers, and talk through strategies to overcome them.
C. Politely let the client know that you are transferring them to another trainer.
D. Let the client know that cancelling sessions costs them money without providing any benefits
cards.back: B. Help the client determine her barriers, and talk through strategies to overcome them.

C. If you spend more time in the gym, you will reach your goals faster.
D. I don't understand why you think it's so hard to do 30 minutes of cardio 3 times a week
cards.back: B. I know that finding time to exercise is hard. I struggle to get it done sometimes as well.

cards.front:
A client reports that he is following a limited diet of chicken and rice every day to avoid eating extra calories from other foods in order to lose weight. What would be an appropriate response within your scope of practice as a fitness professional? Select one:
A. A varied diet of whole foods provides important micronutrients, and this limited diet may be lacking adequate amounts of them.
B. The chicken and rice combination seems adequate to provide caloric, macronutrient, and micronutrient needs.
C. The limited diet sounds like a good plan to limit extra calories from other foods.
D. The diet seems simple enough to maintain for a period of time and facilitate some weight loss
cards.back: A. A varied diet of whole foods provides important micronutrients, and this limited diet may be lacking adequate amounts of them.

Which structure lies anterior to the spleen?
A. Acute cholecystitis
B. Stomach
C. Duodenum, jejunum, ileum
D. Vena cava

Which lobes of the liver are directly separated by the falciform ligament?
A. spleen to the left kidney.
B. The left and right lobes
C. Frontal lobes of the cerebrum
D. Right hepatic duct
cards.back: B. The left and right lobes

cards.front:
Which bile duct drains the bile directly from the largest lobe of the liver?
A. Intralobular duct
B. Hepatic artery
C. Right hepatic duct
D. The left and right lobes

The portal triad, made up of the hepatic artery proper, hepatic portal vein, and common bile duct, is often clamped to control bleeding from the liver in trauma surgery. If bleeding stops with this maneuver, it indicates injury to the hepatic artery or portal vein that may be causing bleeding. If the liver continues to bleed with clamping of the portal triad, what structure is likely injured?
A. Femoral condyles
B. Right hepatic duct
C. Eustachian tubes
D. Hepatic v.

Glucagon is an endocrine hormone produced from which pancreatic cells?
A. Alpha cells
B. myeloid precursor cells.
C. Thromboplastin
D. Luteinizing hormone

Thrombosis of what vessel would result in increased portal vein pressure but normal hepatic sinusoid pressure?
A. Vastus lateralis
B. Portal v.
C. Higher boiling temperature
D. spinal cord.

The lymphatic vessels from the spleen directly drain into which lymph nodes?
A. Superior margin of the talus
B. Gracilis
C. Pancreaticosplenic lymph nodes
D. flexion of the arm

What vessel is adjacent to the head of the pancreas?
A. Inferior mesenteric artery
B. Superior mesenteric a.
C. Superior margin of the talus
D. superior pancreaticoduodenal artery

What is the correct sequence of organs that bile passes through?
A. Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
B. Liver, gall bladder, ampulla of vater, duodenum
C. the brain, neck, and face.
D. liver and the higher right dome of the diaphragm.
cards.back: B. Liver, gall bladder, ampulla of vater, duodenum

cards.front:
A 43 year old woman presents to ED with severe abdominal pain. She has had similar episodes over the past 2 years after eating, but they typically resolve with time. This episode started last night following dinner and has not remitted. The pain is sharp and in her RUQ. She denies fever/chills. Her vitals are within normal limits and confirm she is afebrile. On physical exam, she appears moderately uncomfortable. Her sclera are clear without jaundice or injection. She has tenderness to palpation in her RUQ and arrests respiration with deep palpation of the area. Labs are notable for elevated WBC to 15,000 but have no other abnormalities. A RUQ ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, thickened gall bladder wall, and pericholecystic fluid. What is her most likely diagnosis?
A. Acute cholecystitis
B. Linea aspera
C. Heart
D. Aponeuroses

What best describes renal capsule?
A. Consists of collagen-rich fibrous connective tissue
B. Plasma, platelets, red blood cells, and white blood cells
C. Frontal lobes of the cerebrum
D. Separate a structure from encircling tissue
cards.back: A. Consists of collagen-rich fibrous connective tissue

cards.front:
Which of the following urinary system sequences is the exact urine excretion pathway?
A. Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
B. Lateral corticospinal tract
C. of the diaphragm
D. Renal pelvis, ureters, vladder, urethra
cards.back: D. Renal pelvis, ureters, vladder, urethra

As chyme passes through the gastrointestinal system, it must pass through the ileocecal valve. What portion of the large intestine does this valve pass the chyme into?

What artery supplies nutrients and oxygen to the cervical portion of the esophagus?
A. inferior gluteal nerve

D. Inferior mesenteric a., hindgut

Where in our body can the highly-erosive hydrochloric acid be found?
A. Lateral
B. Deep dorsal v.
C. Stomach
D. 1 through 11.

A 42 year old male with history of anxiety and peptic ulcer disease develops severe back pain. An analysis reveals presence of amylase, lipase, and peptidase in the stomach. This patient's condition is caused by erosion of a peptic ulcer in what structure?
A. Pancreas
B. Vertebral arch
C. Flaring the nostrils
D. Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery

A 67 year old male presents to his physician for annual check up. He has no acute complaints but does admit to increased fatigue, an unintentional 20 lb weight loss over the last year, and worsening constipation. He has never had prior colonoscopy. On physical exam, he appears pale and fatigued but not acutely ill. His abdomen is soft & non tender. His rectal exam is heme-occult negative. He is referred for a colonoscopy where endoscopist discovers a circumferential mass in his sigmoid colon. He undergoes resection of sigmoid colon, Hartmann's pouch creation, and diverting colostomy. What vessel was divided to complete this sigmoid resection and what is its embryological origin?
A. Inferior vena cava
B. Inferior mesenteric a., hindgut
C. Superior mesenteric artery (jejunum)
D. Inferior thyroid a.

Which of the following sequences of the portions of the small intestine is correct?
A. Superior mesenteric artery (jejunum)
B. Duodenum, jejunum, ileum
C. Pulls the central tendon inferiorly
D. Mesovarium

A 28 year old male presents with buffalo hump, thinning arms, hypertension, and diabetes. He is diagnosed with Cushing syndrome. What leads to development of this syndrome when produced in excess?
A. ductless system
B. inferior
C. Cortisol
D. polysaccharide capsule

Which vein emerges from the hilum of the adrenal glands rich with cortisol, norepinephrine, and epinephrine from these glands?
A. Medullary v.
B. Gallbladder
C. Fibrous capsule
D. Superior mesenteric a.

The suprarenal/adrenal glands are located atop the kidneys on either side of the body. Which layer of these organs is responsible for synthesizing most of the androgens by these structures?
A. Descending tract
B. zygomatic nerve (maxillary branch)
C. Zona reticularis
D. metacarpophalangeal joint

D. descending colon

What is the largest component of the hip bone?
A. Ilium
B. Parkinson's disease
C. sagittal
D. Chloride

Injury to the L5 nerve root from a sacral fracture would produce what type of symptoms?
A. descending colon
B. Dysfunction of foot dorsiflexion
C. Ovarian arteries
D. inherited dementia.

How many bones comprise the pelvic girdle?
A. 2
B. Spermatogonia
C. Mechanically-gated channel
D. Natural killer cell

A pregnant woman in labor wants a natural of a birth as possible. Her OBGYN has agreed to accommodate her wishes by giving a local anesthetic to her vaginal vault. What type of pain control is being utilized to her perineum?
A. ball and socket joint
B. of the diaphragm
C. Left atrium
D. Pudendal block

What best describes the function of the scrotum?
A. Tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus
B. Promotes production and viability of sperm
C. Adenine bonds with uracil; guanine bonds with cytosine.
D. It affects mostly males - xlinked
cards.back: B. Promotes production and viability of sperm

cards.front:
What is the correct sequence of the male urethral sections, beginning from innermost?
A. Spongy urethra
B. Internal oblique
C. transferrin
D. Prostatic, membranous, spongy

The obturator artery is a minor artery that supplies the head of the femur at the hip joint. Which ligament encloses this artery?
A. anterior cruciate ligament tear
B. Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
C. Ligament of the head of the femur
D. It affects mostly males - xlinked
cards.back: C. Ligament of the head of the femur

C. Inferior
D. Direct

The hip is considered what type of joint?
A. Ball and socket
B. L4-L5 disk
C. Pyramidalis
D. Pudendal block

A 50 year old woman was ice skating when she fell and damaged the right medial side of her leg. Which area of the leg was damaged?
A. Tibia
B. thiamine deficiency dementia
C. myeloid precursor cells.
D. Vertebral arch

What does the tibial n. pass through before termination in the foot?
A. Inferior mesenteric artery
B. Tarsal tunnel
C. Duodenum
D. Anterior corticospinal tract

A 65 year old male who has recently retired notices pain in his right foot that develops midway through round of golf. He presents to the clinic & is observed to have thickened nails on his right big toe, small ulcer at the ball of his foot (medial side at the head of the first metatarsal), lack of hair on anterior surface of his right ankle & lower leg. An arteriogram reveals occlusive arterial disease in the right popliteal artery just inferior to the adductor hiatus. What is most likely in this patient?
A. upper extremities, with some branches also supplying the head and thorax
B. crenation because the excess sugar will draw fluid from the cell into the insterstitial spaces
C. Branches of femoral a. will provide perfusion to the lower leg
D. Increased pressure in thoracic veins increases the flow of blood into the heart.
cards.back: C. Branches of femoral a. will provide perfusion to the lower leg
